newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek PM says Cyprus has right to buy arms.
newsitem.headline: Greek PM says Cyprus has right to buy arms.

text.p: Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis said on Monday that Cyprus had the right to boost its defence and dismissed Turkish threats to strike at a planned Russian missile system on the island.
"Cyprus is an independent state. It is free to decide on its defence and on the weapons it will use to get results," he told reporters after meeting his foreign and defence ministers.

Turkey has warned Cyprus that it could strike at the S-300 anti-aircraft system if deployed and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash threatened to integrate a disputed no-man's land into the Turkish sector of the island.

"Those who are concerned (Turkey) don't have to do much. Just end the illegal occupation of Cyprus and contribute to the Cypriot government's proposal for a demilitarisation of the island," Simitis said.
He said Greece was determined to keep its composure in facing Turkish threats and would not give in to a climate of crisis.

Turkey invaded Cyprus in 1974 after a brief Greek Cypriot coup inspired by the military then ruling Athens. Around 30,000 troops are based in north Cyprus, declared a Turkish Cypriot state in 1983 but recognised only by Ankara.

"These offensive missiles will definitely not be deployed. If they are deployed we will do what is needed, if that means they need to be hit they will be hit," Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said last week.

U.S. state department spokesman Nicholas Burns issued two warnings to Turkey over the threat to use force and said that although Washington was against the deployment of the missiles, Ankara should not resort to military force.
Burns said the S-300, which could hurt Turkish air superiority over the militarily divided island, did not contribute to efforts to reach a peaceful solution.

Greece and Cyprus have brushed off the criticism, saying it was a double standard to worry about a purely defensive system in the south while allowing 30,000 heavily armed Turkish troops in the north.
In an effort to ease the tension Washington has sent senior diplomat Carey Cavanaugh, who heads the State Department's office of southern European affairs, to visit Nicosia, Athens and Ankara.
Cavanaugh arrives in Athens from Nicosia later on Monday and is expected to fly to Turkey on Wednesday after talks with Greek officials.
Simitis said he would meet in Athens on Friday with Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides "to review our common policy".
